html:
The Shan States were many small Tai principalities in the hills of what is now north-eastern Myanmar (Burma), each called a möng and ruled by a prince called a saopha, "lord of the sky". The map shows them from 1530 to 1715.

The Shan are Tai people, related to the Thai and Lao. Their chronicles date the first Shan states to the early 1200s, part of the same Tai movement that founded the Ahom kingdom in Assam and Sukhothai in Siam. After the Mongols broke Pagan in 1287, Shan lords dominated Upper Burma for nearly three centuries. In 1527 a Shan alliance even took the Burmese capital, Ava.

That ended with the Taungoo kings. Bayinnaung took Ava in 1555 and brought the Shan States under Burmese overlordship over the next few years. From then on, through the years on the map, the saophas kept their own courts and laws but paid tribute to Burma, while some eastern states also looked to Ming China.

Under British rule the Shan States were kept as semi-independent princely lands. The saophas gave up their powers in 1959.
